summary:
**Conversation Overview**

This was a long, generative working session with a professor and Co-Director of the AI Exploration (AIX) Center at SUNY Polytechnic Institute who has been teaching there for approximately 35 years. The person works in communication, hypertext theory, and computer-mediated discourse, and is developing an RTW (Reading, Thinking, Writing with AI) framework as their core pedagogical and research practice. The session had two intertwined threads running simultaneously: drafting an introductory letter to IDT (Information Design & Technology) program students, and a wide-ranging exploratory conversation about AI research projects, model training, STS (Science, Technology, and Society) scholarship, and Empire AI infrastructure.

The letter was built incrementally through the conversation, with the person dictating structure, content, and corrections as Claude drafted. Key structural decisions included: opening with the person's own words (not Claude's), placing "A Community of AI" up front, removing the person's name and SUNY AI Fellow affiliation, framing courses as research and development opportunities rather than classes, and omitting IDT 507 from the final version. The letter was ultimately rendered as a tabbed HTML file matching the visual design of an existing Herkimer County artifact, with four tabs: Welcome, Summer of AIX, Research Ecosystem, and Graduate Assistants. The file was saved to ~/tilde-steve/artifacts/ and the person was given git commands to commit and push it to their GitHub repo.

Research projects documented in the letter include: Herkimer County AI Governance Initiative (seven-dimension framework, policy validation work), Analytic Capabilities citation network (starting from the Burkina Faso anchor paper), FYS 111 AI literacy curriculum (open educational resource, Brightspace cartridge deliverable), AI and the Human Future course development (STS-grounded, Zotero annotated bibliography as capstone opportunity), Legal and Ethical Issues in the Information Age (Maslow hierarchy as organizing lens, cube/voxel resource architecture as capstone opportunity), NYHIMA workshop design (three-hour workshop for New York Health Information Management Association, early June deadline), Open Educational Resources and AI training materials, and Africa Partnerships grounded in the COIL (Collaborative Online International Learning) framework with institutions in Nigeria and Cameroon. Three GA positions were defined: AIX Communications & Research (10–20 hrs/week), LLM Validation & Verification Research (10–12 hrs/week, spanning Herkimer, OER, and analytic capabilities), and Production Pipeline Manager.

A significant portion of the conversation was a genuine intellectual exploration of whether and how to build discipline-specific fine-tuned language models, starting with STS. The person worked through the distinction between RAG and fine-tuning, the IP constraints around training data, the role of synthetic data as a workaround, and the potential use of Empire AI (a New York State GPU computing consortium anchored at Stony Brook, Buffalo, Cornell, NYU, Columbia, and Rensselaer, funded partly by the Simons Foundation). A key insight reached was that a Stony Brook collaboration would unlock Empire AI access for SUNY Poly, and that the STS model project could serve as Empire AI's humanities/social science use case. The person concluded that the immediate STS project is building the "AI and the Human Future" course knowledge base collaboratively, using open-access materials and scholar contributions as anchors, with frontier models as intermediaries for synthetic data generation. The person explicitly noted they are an outsider to STS as a formal discipline and are entering it as a learner.

Key colleagues mentioned: Bill (collaborator on the analytic capabilities/DAC-AC project, postdoctoral hire), Todd (STS professor at Stony Brook, met at a recent SUNY AI Symposium lunch, contact info in phone photos), and Dianne (whose students are a candidate pool for STS instructional design hire). The person works across Teams, Discord, and is considering how to bring Discord's community feel into Teams through behavior and structure rather than switching platforms.

# A Letter to IDT Students
**Steve Quigley · AIX Center · SUNY Polytechnic Institute · Spring 2026**

---

What does it mean to read, think, and write *with* AI rather than *around* it?

That's not a rhetorical question. It's the question I come back to every day — in my research, in how I prepare for class, in how I'm writing this letter right now. I don't have a settled answer, and I'm not sure I want one. What I have is a practice, a framework I call RTW — Reading, Thinking, Writing with AI — and a deep conviction that the most interesting work in our field right now happens at that edge where human judgment meets machine inference.

I'm Steve Quigley. I'm a professor here at SUNY Poly, Co-Director of the AI Exploration (AIX) Center, and SUNY AI for the Public Good Fellow for 2025–2026. My background is in communication, hypertext theory, and computer-mediated discourse — which is a long way of saying I've been watching humans and networks think together for over twenty years, and I've never found the moment more interesting than right now.

I'm writing because I'll be teaching in the IDT program starting this fall, and because I want to open a real conversation with you before we ever sit down in a classroom together.

---

## The Research Ecosystem — and Where You Might Fit

The AIX Center isn't a typical academic unit. It's a working lab — projects with real clients, real stakes, and real opportunities for students to contribute in meaningful ways. Below is a map of what's active right now. Each project has room for students, and the entry points vary: some are course-based, some are independent study or capstone territory, some are paid assistantships. I'll say more about pathways at the end of this letter.

### Herkimer County AI Governance Initiative

Herkimer County has invited the AIX Center to help them think through what responsible AI adoption looks like for a rural county government. We've developed a seven-dimension framework — three Framing dimensions (Equity, Human Impact, Infrastructure Impact) that set the county's overall posture, and four Operational dimensions (Security, Efficiency, Innovation, Accountability) that can be calibrated Hi or Lo for specific policy decisions.

We're now in working sessions with county leadership, moving from framework to policy. The research opportunities here are concrete: policy analysis and drafting, validation of AI governance policies for consistency with the framework, documentation of tools and workflows, facilitation support for working sessions. If you're interested in how institutions actually navigate AI adoption — not in theory but in practice — this is the project.

*Skills of value: analytical writing, policy analysis, attention to detail, comfort with ambiguity.*

### Analytic Capabilities — Citation Network and Digital Library Construction

This project supports the development of an analytical framework for societal vulnerability analysis, grounded in political science and used to understand conditions that precede institutional instability. The immediate research task is building out a citation network — starting from a key anchor paper and mapping connections forward, backward, and sideways across the literature. It's part digital library construction, part intellectual cartography.

Much of this work is machine-assisted, and it would benefit enormously from someone with library science instincts or connections to librarian resources. If you like finding the shape of a field, this project is for you.

*Skills of value: research methods, information organization, comfort with AI-assisted literature tools.*

### AI Literacy Curriculum — FYS 111

We are building the AI literacy curriculum for SUNY Poly's First Year Seminar from the ground up — slides, exercises, activities, and assessments — as an open educational resource. This is collaborative by design: students who join this project help shape what thousands of first-year students will encounter as their first formal introduction to AI in higher education.

This work can be framed as independent study, as a capstone project, or simply as a contribution you propose on your own terms.

*Skills of value: instructional design, writing, curriculum development, interest in pedagogy.*

### AI and the Human Future — Course and Knowledge Base Development

I am building a new course — working title "AI and the Human Future" — grounded in Science, Technology, and Society (STS) frameworks. STS, as I'm interpreting it for this course, means taking seriously the entire social, technical, and cultural system that AI is embedded in: Where does AI come from? Who built it, and why? What do economists, political scientists, philosophers, linguists, and theologians have to say about AI and what it means for us?

I'm new to STS as a formal discipline, and I'm building this course as a learner, not an expert. That's where students come in. The project involves identifying leading textbooks, mapping core topics, and constructing a participatory knowledge base — something like a wiki-education approach to the discipline. I need someone who can help design an engaging introductory course precisely because they're not already inside the field.

*Skills of value: curiosity, research, instructional design, comfort working at the edges of your knowledge.*

### Open Educational Resources and AI Training Materials

The AIX Center contributes to a growing ecosystem of open educational resources for AI literacy across the SUNY system and beyond. There is ongoing work in developing workshop materials, training modules, and documentation — including the AIX Workbench, AI Learner's Permit, and Exploring AI Agents short course series. Students who join this work get a behind-the-scenes view of how professional development around AI actually gets designed and delivered.

*Skills of value: writing, instructional design, workshop facilitation, documentation.*

### Africa Partnerships — Nigeria and Cameroon

The AIX Center maintains active academic partnerships with institutions in Nigeria and Cameroon, with work focused on AI literacy, curriculum development, and institutional capacity. There are opportunities for students interested in international education, comparative AI policy, and the global dimensions of the AI literacy challenge.

*Skills of value: research, writing, cross-cultural communication, interest in international education.*

---

## The Courses

### Fall 2026 — Legal and Ethical Issues in the Information Age

This course will use AI as both the *object* of study and the *method* of study. We'll ask: what legal and ethical frameworks do we actually need to navigate the information age? And we'll ask that question at every scale — from the choices you make about your own data, to how organizations govern AI use, to the state and federal legislative landscape (which is moving fast right now), to the planetary-scale questions that nation-state frameworks aren't built to answer.

One organizing thread I'm developing: Maslow's hierarchy of needs as a lens on information ethics. Security and privacy map onto safety needs. Belonging and identity get complicated by platforms and algorithmic curation. Self-actualization runs up against intellectual freedom and access. It's not a perfect framework — no framework is — but it's a productive one for asking: *what do humans actually need from the information systems we're building?*

The course will be AI-forward. I'll be reading, thinking, and writing with AI throughout, and I'll ask you to do the same — and to reflect critically on what that experience is like.

### Spring 2027 — IDT 507

More to come on this one, but the design philosophy is already clear: this is a course where you navigate your own path. I'll bring frameworks, provocations, and real research problems. You'll bring your interests, your questions, and your own sense of what you want to make. Assignments are crafted in dialogue, not handed down. If that sounds like the kind of learning you're looking for, keep an eye on this one.

---

## How to Get Involved

There are several ways to engage with this work, and they're not mutually exclusive:

**Enrolled courses** — the most straightforward path, fall and spring.

**Independent study or capstone** — if you have a research question that connects to any of the projects above, we can design a course of study around it. This is especially appropriate for students who want to go deep on one project and produce something substantial.

**Paid graduate assistantship** — a limited number of paid positions are available across projects. These are research-intensive roles that require consistent engagement and clear deliverables.

**Unpaid participation** — some students want to contribute and learn without the formality of credit or pay. That's a legitimate path too, and you're welcome.

---

## Summer of AI in AIX

The summer isn't dead time — it's actually when some of the most interesting work happens. Here's what's available this summer:

**Living with AI — Tuesday nights online.** A weekly demo series where people share what they're actually doing with AI. Low-key, participatory, open. If you want to present something you're working on, there will be a way to sign up.

**Pizza nights on campus — probably Wednesdays.** Show up, eat, talk about what you're building.

**Launch-on-demand short courses.** We'll run these when there's enough interest — no fixed schedule, just sign up and we'll launch:
- *AIX Workbench* — 3 sessions
- *Exploring AI Agents* — 3 sessions
- *AI Learner's Permit* — 2 sessions (pre/post)

All Teams-based, lunch/learn format, designed to fit into a working day.

---

## A Note on How I Teach

I don't believe in a single right answer to the question of how to work with AI. I use the RTW framework — Reading, Thinking, Writing — because it reflects how I actually work, not because it's the only way. In my courses, I'll be transparent about my own process, including where it's uncertain or still developing.

What I'll ask of you is similar transparency. I want to know how you think, where your instincts lead you, and how AI does or doesn't fit into that. Assignments in my courses are designed to be navigated, not just completed. If you have a different way in — a different question, a different form, a different approach — bring it. We'll figure out together whether it works.

This letter is an invitation to show up as yourself in this work.

I look forward to meeting you.

---

**Steve Quigley**
Professor, Communication and IDT
Co-Director, AIX Center
SUNY AI for the Public Good Fellow, 2025–2026
SUNY Polytechnic Institute

# A Letter to IDT Students
**AIX Center · SUNY Polytechnic Institute · Spring 2026**

---

## A Community of AI

Underlying everything in this letter is something simpler: an invitation to think together. The questions AI raises — about knowledge, about work, about what it means to be human in a world of increasingly capable machines — are not questions any of us can answer alone. The AIX Center is a community as much as a research unit, and what makes it work is people who are genuinely curious, willing to share what they're learning, and open to being surprised.

That's the kind of student I'm hoping to meet. Read on.

---

I'm writing to invite you to participate in a journey of exploring artificial intelligence as you complete your degree in Information Design & Technology.

As some of you know, I've embraced using generative AI as a tool for teaching and learning over the past few semesters, and I'll continue to adjust my approach. As I prepare for a summer of reading, reflection, and research — and in preparation for teaching two IDT courses next year — I'll be reconsidering and likely refining how I work. I'd welcome your feedback and reflection throughout.

My framework for working with AI is something I call RTW — Reading, Thinking, Writing with AI. It's not a doctrine; it's a practice, and it's still developing. What I believe, and what I'd invite you to test for yourself, is that the most interesting work happens at the edge where human judgment meets machine inference. That edge is what this letter is about.

I'm a professor here at SUNY Poly and Co-Director of the AI Exploration (AIX) Center, where we work at the intersection of AI literacy, research, and real-world application.

---

## Summer of AI in AIX

The summer isn't dead time — it's actually when some of the most interesting work happens. Here's what's available right now:

**Open Mic AI — Tuesday nights online.** Show and tell, or just talk and listen. People share what they're actually doing with AI — a tool they tried, a project they're working on, something that surprised them, something that didn't work. Low-key, participatory, no agenda. If you want to take the mic, you're welcome to.

**Pizza nights on campus — probably Wednesdays.** Show up, eat, talk about what you're building.

**Getting up to speed with AI — on-demand short courses.** Anytime four students are ready to go, we launch. Each course runs three sessions: Getting Started, Moving Forward, Wrapping Up. Choose from:
- *Exploring AI Chatbots*
- *Exploring AI Agents*
- *Building My AI Workbench*

Teams-based, lunch/learn format, designed to fit into a working day.

---

The AIX Center is a working lab — projects with real clients, real stakes, and real opportunities for students to contribute in meaningful ways. Below is a map of what's active right now.

**How to engage:** Email to ask about a project. See if there's a capstone, independent study, or course-related project that fits. Take a short course to get started with skills and engagement. Or ask about one of the summer graduate assistant positions described at the end of this letter.

---

### Herkimer County AI Governance Initiative

Herkimer County has invited the AIX Center to help them think through what responsible AI adoption looks like for a rural county government. We've developed a seven-dimension framework — three Framing dimensions (Equity, Human Impact, Infrastructure Impact) that set the county's overall posture, and four Operational dimensions (Security, Efficiency, Innovation, Accountability) that can be calibrated Hi or Lo for specific policy decisions. We're now in working sessions with county leadership, moving from framework to policy.

*Skills of value: analytical writing, policy analysis, attention to detail, comfort with ambiguity.*

---

### Analytic Capabilities — Citation Network and Digital Library Construction

*Skills of value: research methods, information organization, comfort with AI-assisted literature tools, interest in epistemology and knowledge quality.*

We are building the AI literacy curriculum for SUNY Poly's First Year Seminar from the ground up — slides, exercises, activities, and assessments — as an open educational resource. Students who join this project help shape what thousands of first-year students will encounter as their first formal introduction to AI in higher education.

*Skills of value: instructional design, writing, curriculum development, interest in pedagogy and learning management systems.*

It asks not just how things work, but who built them, under what pressures, for whose benefit, and with what consequences. It draws on history, philosophy, sociology, anthropology, and cultural theory to understand technology as something that is always already political, always already embedded in systems of power and meaning.

I am building a new course grounded in that tradition — working title "AI and the Human Future" — that takes AI as its subject and asks the STS questions seriously. I'm building this course as a learner, not an STS expert.

This combines information architecture, library science practice, and instructional design into a single deliverable that will be used immediately.

*Skills of value: curiosity, research, information architecture, instructional design, comfort working at the edges of your knowledge.*

---

The legal and ethical landscape around AI and information technology is moving fast — data center moratoriums, state versus federal preemption battles, child safety legislation, consumer protection frameworks. This is both a course under development and an ongoing research project. We're building a working understanding of that landscape in real time, tracking legislation, analyzing frameworks, and developing case studies.

One organizing thread under development: Maslow's hierarchy of needs as a lens on information ethics — security and privacy at the safety level, identity and belonging complicated by platforms and algorithmic curation, self-actualization running up against intellectual freedom and access.

The goal is a navigable resource architecture for the course that can be traversed in multiple directions rather than consumed linearly.

*Skills of value: research, legal and policy analysis, information architecture, writing, comfort with fast-moving material.*

---

### Workshop Design — NYHIMA and AI Training Materials

We are designing and co-delivering a three-hour AI literacy workshop for the New York Health Information Management Association — practitioners who work at the intersection of healthcare, data, and technology. This is a real audience, a real deadline (early June), and a real deliverable: curriculum design from scratch, built for professionals navigating AI adoption in a regulated, high-stakes field.

This project connects to the broader AIX open educational resource ecosystem — workshop materials, training modules, and documentation including the AIX Workbench, Exploring AI Chatbots, Exploring AI Agents, and Building My AI Workbench short course series.

**Capstone or independent study opportunity:** Design the full NYHIMA workshop as an instructional design project — learning objectives, instructional design objects, facilitation guide, and participant materials. *Skills of value: instructional design, facilitation, writing, interest in health informatics or professional development.*

---

### Africa Partnerships — COIL and International AI Literacy

The AIX Center maintains active academic partnerships with institutions in Nigeria and Cameroon, with work focused on AI literacy, curriculum development, and institutional capacity. This work is grounded in the COIL framework — Collaborative Online International Learning — which creates structured opportunities for cross-institutional engagement between students and faculty across contexts.

COIL itself is a rich IDT topic: designing learning experiences that work across time zones, cultures, languages, and institutional contexts is a genuine instructional design challenge with growing relevance as AI tools reshape what's possible in international collaboration.

**Capstone or independent study opportunity:** Design and implement a COIL experience focused on AI literacy in collaboration with a partner institution in Nigeria or Cameroon. Or develop a capstone examining COIL as an instructional design framework — its affordances, constraints, and future directions in an AI-enabled environment.

*Skills of value: research, writing, cross-cultural communication, instructional design, interest in international and collaborative learning.*

---

## Graduate Assistant Positions

### GA — AIX Communications & Research (10–20 hrs/week)

Manage digital communication platforms (Discord, Teams, website, podcast), curate workshop and course materials, support accessible web content for AIX, coordinate outreach and communication strategy, and document ongoing research and teaching activities. Strong writing and organizational skills required. Interest in AI, media design, and accessibility best practices.

### GA — LLM Validation & Verification Research (10–12 hrs/week)

Develop and implement protocols for the validation and verification of text generated by large language models across three active AIX projects: AI governance policy formulation (Herkimer County), open educational resource development (AI literacy curriculum), and societal vulnerability analysis (analytic capabilities framework).

LLM-generated materials raise specific and consequential questions about accuracy, consistency, and fitness for purpose. This GA will design systematic protocols for evaluating those materials — checking factual claims, assessing internal consistency, verifying alignment with source frameworks, and documenting where and how AI-generated content meets or falls short of standards required for real-world use. The work is methodological as much as editorial: you're not just proofreading, you're building a replicable approach to quality assurance in LLM-assisted research and curriculum production.

*Skills of value: analytical rigor, technical writing, research methods, attention to detail, interest in AI reliability and accountability.*

### GA — Production Pipeline Manager

Design and manage the production pipeline for materials developed with LLMs across AIX projects. Map existing workflows, identify where LLMs are integrated into content production, and design pipeline architecture that ensures materials move efficiently from prompt to draft to review to publication. Maintain version control, document tool choices and prompting strategies, coordinate handoffs between contributors, and ensure production processes are transparent and transferable. This is a design and systems role — the ideal candidate thinks in workflows.

*Skills of value: systems thinking, project management, workflow design, familiarity with digital production tools, interest in AI-assisted content development.*

---

## How to Get Involved

**Take a short course** to build skills and get oriented — any of the three on-demand courses launch when four students are ready.

**Email to ask about a project** — describe your interests and background, and we'll figure out together whether there's a fit as a capstone, independent study, course project, or assistantship.

**Enrolled courses** — Legal and Ethical Issues in the Information Age (fall) and IDT 507 (spring) are both designed as research and development experiences, not just classes.

**Independent study or capstone** — if your interests connect to any project above, we can design a course of study around your specific question and deliverable.

**Paid graduate assistantship** — three positions available this summer, described above.

**Unpaid participation** — some students want to contribute and learn without the formality of credit or pay. That's a legitimate path too, and you're welcome.

---

I look forward to the conversation.

---

**Professor, Communication and IDT**
**Co-Director, AIX Center**
**SUNY Polytechnic Institute**
